chapters.1: Moses begins his farewell address to Israel in Moab, just before they cross the Jordan, by reviewing their journey from Horeb. He recalls appointing judges and leaders to help carry the burden of the people, and retells how the generation that left Egypt refused to enter Canaan after the spies' bad report, so God sentenced them to wander forty years in the wilderness instead.
chapters.2: Moses continues recounting the wilderness journey, including how Israel was told not to provoke the descendants of Esau or Moab since God had given them their own lands. He describes Israel's path around Edom and Moab and the defeat of King Sihon of the Amorites, whose land and cities Israel captured and destroyed.
chapters.3: Moses recalls Israel's victory over Og, the giant king of Bashan, and the capture of sixty of his cities. He describes dividing the conquered land east of the Jordan among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, and tells how he pleaded with God to let him cross into Canaan but was only allowed to view it from a distance, with Joshua appointed to lead the people in.
chapters.4: Moses urges Israel to obey God's laws carefully, without adding to or subtracting from them, pointing to the disaster at Baal-peor as proof of what happens when they don't. He warns against idolatry, especially making images of God, and reminds them that God chose and rescued them uniquely among the nations; the chapter ends by noting cities of refuge Moses set apart east of the Jordan.
chapters.5: Moses restates the Ten Commandments that God gave at Horeb, reminding the people that this covenant is with them personally, not just their ancestors. He recalls how the people were afraid of God's direct voice and asked Moses to be their mediator, and he urges them to keep every command so they may live long and do well in the land.
chapters.6: Moses gives the central command to love the Lord with all one's heart, soul, and strength, and to keep these words constantly in mind, teaching them to children and marking them in daily life. He warns against forgetting God once they are settled and prosperous in the new land, and against following the gods of the surrounding peoples.
chapters.7: Moses instructs Israel to completely drive out and show no mercy to the seven nations of Canaan, avoiding intermarriage and alliances that could lead them into idolatry. He explains that God chose Israel not because of their size or merit but out of love and faithfulness to his promise to their ancestors, and he assures them God will give them victory if they obey.
chapters.8: Moses tells Israel to remember how God humbled and tested them in the wilderness, feeding them manna to teach that people live by God's word, not bread alone. He warns that once they enjoy the good land's abundance, they must not forget the Lord who brought them out of Egypt and gave them everything they have.
chapters.9: Moses warns Israel not to credit their coming conquest to their own righteousness, since they are a stubborn people; God is driving out the nations because of those nations' wickedness and to keep his promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He retells the golden calf incident at Horeb and how he interceded for the people to keep God from destroying them.
chapters.10: Moses recounts making new stone tablets after breaking the first ones, and placing them in the ark; he notes Aaron's death and the Levites being set apart for priestly service with no land inheritance of their own. He closes by calling Israel to fear God, love him, and treat strangers with kindness, since Israel themselves were once strangers in Egypt.
chapters.11: Moses reminds the people that they personally witnessed God's power in Egypt and in the wilderness, unlike their children. He sets before them a choice between blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience as they enter the land, and tells them to keep God's words constantly before them, teaching them to their children.
chapters.12: Moses commands Israel to destroy all Canaanite places of worship and to bring their sacrifices, tithes, and offerings only to the one place God will choose for his name, rather than worshiping however they please. He warns them not to adopt Canaanite religious practices when they settle in the land.
chapters.13: Moses warns against following any prophet or dream-interpreter who tries to lead Israel after other gods, even if their predictions come true; such a person is to be put to death. The same applies even to a close family member who secretly tries to turn someone to idolatry, and an entire city that turns to idol worship is to be destroyed.
chapters.14: Moses forbids pagan mourning customs and lists which animals, birds, and water creatures are clean and may be eaten and which are unclean and forbidden. The chapter also covers tithing a tenth of produce each year, part of which supports Levites, the poor, and festive worship before the Lord.
chapters.15: Moses establishes a seven-year cycle in which debts owed by fellow Israelites are to be released, and commands generous, free-hearted lending to the poor without resentment. He also addresses the freeing of Hebrew slaves in the seventh year, sending them off with provisions, and rules about dedicating firstborn animals.
chapters.16: Moses reviews the three annual pilgrimage festivals: Passover/Unleavened Bread commemorating the exodus, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) tied to the harvest, and the Feast of Tabernacles, all to be celebrated at the place God chooses. He also instructs Israel to appoint fair judges and warns against bribery and setting up idolatrous pillars or images.
chapters.17: Moses gives rules for dealing with idolaters, who are to be stoned on the testimony of multiple witnesses, and for handling difficult legal cases by bringing them to the priests and judges at the central sanctuary. He also lays out guidelines for a future king, limiting his wealth, wives, and foreign alliances, and requiring him to read and follow God's law.
chapters.18: Moses explains that the Levites and priests receive no land inheritance because their portion is serving the Lord and living from the offerings. He condemns pagan practices like divination and sorcery, and promises that God will raise up a prophet like Moses whom the people must listen to, while warning against false prophets.
chapters.19: Moses commands Israel to set aside cities of refuge where someone who kills another person accidentally can flee for safety from revenge, distinguishing this from deliberate murder, which still carries the death penalty. He also requires at least two or three witnesses to establish guilt in any case, and prescribes punishment for false witnesses.
chapters.20: Moses gives rules for warfare, including exemptions from fighting for men who have just built a house, planted a vineyard, gotten engaged, or who are simply afraid. He distinguishes how Israel is to treat distant cities, offering terms of peace or surrender, from the Canaanite nations in the land itself, which are to be completely destroyed.
chapters.21: Moses provides a ritual for atoning for an unsolved murder by the nearest town's elders, and rules protecting a captured foreign wife's dignity and a firstborn son's inheritance rights even if his mother is less favored. The chapter also covers the harsh treatment of a persistently rebellious son and the burial of an executed criminal.
chapters.22: Moses gives a wide range of everyday civil and moral laws, including returning lost property, helping an animal that has fallen, not cross-dressing, protecting bird nests, building safety rails on rooftops, and avoiding mixing certain things (seeds, animals, fabrics). It also addresses laws about marital fidelity, virginity claims, and adultery.
chapters.23: Moses lists who may and may not be admitted into the assembly of Israel, including restrictions on Ammonites and Moabites because of their past hostility. He also covers camp cleanliness and purity during war, the fair treatment of escaped slaves, prohibitions on charging fellow Israelites interest, and rules about vows and gleaning in a neighbor's field.
chapters.24: Moses gives regulations on divorce and remarriage, exempting newly married men from military service, and prohibiting taking a millstone as loan collateral since it's essential for a family's livelihood. He also forbids kidnapping for slavery, requires prompt payment of wages to the poor, and commands leaving some harvest in the fields for the poor, widows, and foreigners.
chapters.25: Moses sets limits on corporal punishment in legal disputes and establishes the custom of levirate marriage, where a man marries his deceased brother's childless widow to preserve the family line, including a public shaming ritual if he refuses. The chapter also commands honest weights and measures and recalls Israel's command to later deal with the Amalekites for attacking them during the exodus.
chapters.26: Moses instructs Israel that once settled in the land, they are to bring the first fruits of their harvest to the sanctuary with a recitation recalling their journey from slavery in Egypt to the promised land. He also describes a triennial tithe set aside for Levites, orphans, widows, and foreigners, confirming Israel's covenant commitment to follow God's laws.
chapters.27: Moses and the elders instruct the people to set up large inscribed stones on Mount Ebal once they cross the Jordan, and to build an altar there for offerings. The Levites are to pronounce a series of curses from the mountains of Ebal and Gerizim against specific sins such as idolatry, dishonoring parents, and sexual immorality, with the people responding "amen."
chapters.28: Moses lays out in detail the blessings that will come from obeying God — prosperity, protection, and prominence among nations — and the much longer list of curses that will come from disobedience, including disease, defeat, drought, exile, and desperate suffering. This chapter functions as the covenant's core statement of consequences for Israel's future choices.
chapters.29: Moses calls the whole nation, from leaders to the lowest servant, to formally enter into covenant with God as they stand on the plains of Moab. He warns that anyone who secretly turns to idolatry while claiming peace with God invites disaster, and that future generations who break the covenant will see their land desolated like an overturned city.
chapters.30: Moses promises that even after exile for disobedience, if Israel returns to God wholeheartedly, he will restore and bless them again, circumcising their hearts to love him fully. He famously sets before the people a clear choice between life and death, blessing and curse, and urges them to choose life by loving and obeying the Lord.
chapters.31: At 120 years old, Moses announces he will not cross the Jordan and formally commissions Joshua as his successor, encouraging him and the people to be strong and unafraid since God will go with them. Moses writes down the law, has it read publicly every seven years, and God warns him that Israel will eventually turn to other gods despite everything.
chapters.32: This chapter contains the "Song of Moses," a poetic recounting of God's faithfulness to Israel contrasted with Israel's future unfaithfulness and the judgment that will follow, along with God's promise to ultimately vindicate his people. Afterward, God tells Moses to go up Mount Nebo, where he will see the promised land before he dies.
chapters.33: Before his death, Moses pronounces a blessing over each of the twelve tribes of Israel, addressing their individual character, future territory, and role among the people. The chapter closes with praise of Israel's unique security under God, who is described as riding to their help and being their eternal refuge.
chapters.34: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, where God shows him the entire promised land he will not personally enter, and Moses dies there in Moab at 120 years old, still strong and clear-sighted. Israel mourns him for thirty days, Joshua takes over leadership full of wisdom, and the book closes by honoring Moses as a prophet unlike any other, who knew God face to face.
